analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare Advantage insurers to use electronic prior authorization and publish their denial data.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 231 House cosponsors — more than half the chamber — never got a committee vote or floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force Medicare Advantage plans, the private insurance alternative to traditional Medicare that covers most new Medicare enrollees, to modernize how they handle prior authorization — the process where an insurer must approve a treatment or test before a doctor can provide it. Starting in 2026, plans would have to report publicly each year what they require prior authorization for, how many requests they approve or deny, how often denials are overturned on appeal, how quickly they decide, and how much they rely on artificial intelligence to make those calls. Starting in 2027, plans would have to accept and answer prior authorization requests through a standardized secure electronic system rather than fax or proprietary portals, and could face shorter deadlines for responding to requests. It would also require plans to disclose their approval criteria to providers and to enrollees who ask.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled people enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, who today can wait days or weeks for approval of care or be denied it, and their doctors, who juggle fax machines and plan-specific portals to get approvals. More than half the Medicare population is in Medicare Advantage plans, so slow or opaque denials touch millions of people.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Advantage enrollees and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Plans would have to report to HHS each year, and HHS would publish on a public CMS website, the list of items and services requiring prior authorization, approval and denial rates by item or service, how many denials were appealed and how many appeals succeeded, and average and median decision times in hours [S2].

Plans would have to disclose how much they use artificial intelligence, machine learning, or other decision-support technology in making coverage determinations, and describe that technology — a response to reports that insurers use algorithms to help deny care [S2].

Beginning with plan years starting on or after January 1, 2027, every plan using prior authorization would have to run a standardized electronic program, excluding fax and non-compliant proprietary portals, with technical standards set by the Secretary [S2].

The Secretary could set shorter response deadlines, such as 24 hours, for expedited requests, real-time decisions on routinely approved services, and other requests, tightening the current 72-hour window [S2].

Plans would have to give providers and suppliers the plan's coverage criteria and required documentation up front, and give enrollees access to the criteria used to decide their own care upon request [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurance companies, which would build and maintain electronic prior authorization systems, compile and publish detailed annual denial and AI-use data, disclose their approval criteria, and in many cases approve care faster — which cuts into a tool they use to manage costs. Some of that compliance cost could show up in plan premiums or in stricter plan offerings.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: insurers and some providers argue prior authorization exists to prevent overuse and inappropriate care, and faster automatic approvals plus exemptions for high-performing providers could allow more low-value care, pushing costs into plan bids and Medicare payments [S2].

Compliance is a real cost: plans would have to build standardized electronic systems and compile granular annual data on every item and service, and smaller plans or providers could face transition burdens while the 2026-2027 phase-in takes effect [S2].

The bill relies heavily on transparency rather than prohibition — it requires plans to report denials and AI use but does not ban any denial practice outright, so critics could fairly say it creates paperwork without directly stopping improper denials [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for enrollees are concrete: public denial data, disclosed criteria, faster electronic decisions, and scrutiny of AI-driven denials address real, well-documented access problems in Medicare Advantage. The costs are administrative and fall mostly on insurers, some of which could pass through to premiums. The bill's main design weakness is that it leans on sunlight and process rather than hard prohibitions, but for a bill aiming at a giant industry, that is a deliberate, defensible trade-off rather than a flaw that undermines its purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2024 and sent to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, then referred to a Ways and Means health subcommittee in December, and never reached a committee vote or the House floor before Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S4].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 12, 2024, by Rep. Mike Kelly (R-PA) with an initial bipartisan group of over 100 cosponsors listed on the bill [S1][S2].
It was referred to two committees — Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce — meaning either or both would have had to act on it before any floor vote [S4].

On December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, a step that typically means the full committee had not taken it up; the Congress ended about two weeks later with no further action [S4].
Despite 231 cosponsors — 140 of 216 House Democrats and 91 of 224 House Republicans, a majority of the full chamber — the bill never received a vote in committee or on the floor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers are better off: they avoided mandatory electronic prior authorization, public denial data, and AI-use disclosure, and keep the current opaque process.

for.name: Mike Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized a large bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: 231 House cosponsors
for.role: Majority of the House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — 140 of 216 House Democrats and 91 of 224 House Republicans.

for.name: Physicians and provider groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly endorsed prior authorization reform legislation of this kind in past Congresses, citing fax-based approvals and slow plan responses as burdens on patient care.

against.name: Mike Johnson

against.name: Medicare Advantage insurance industry
against.role: Health insurers offering Medicare Advantage plans (UnitedHealth, Humana, CVS/Aetna, etc.)
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory restrictions on prior authorization, arguing it controls improper utilization and costs, and supported voluntary electronic standards instead.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 140 of 216 House Democrats and 91 of 224 House Republicans cosponsored, a majority of the full chamber — but the bill died under House Republican control without a vote.

industries.note: These insurers would have to build electronic prior authorization systems, publish denial and AI-use data, disclose coverage criteria, and respond faster — shrinking their discretion to delay or deny care, which is a lever they use to control costs. Their interest in keeping the process opaque runs against enrollees waiting for care.

Providers would get standardized electronic approvals instead of faxes and plan-specific portals, access to plans' approval criteria up front, and possible exemptions from prior authorization based on their track record — less paperwork and faster answers for their patients.

industries.industry: Health IT and electronic prior authorization vendors
industries.note: The bill mandates a standardized electronic prior authorization system by 2027, creating demand for the software and interoperability services that would run it, under standards the Secretary would set.
